title: Haematuria with LUTS (Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia)
patient_instructions: You are Barry Whitfield, a 55-year-old carpenter who has come to your GP because you noticed your urine has turned red/pink over the last week. You are frightened it might be cancer because your father died of a bladder problem. If asked, the redness is there most times you pass urine and you have seen a couple of small clots. Over the past few months you have also had to get up 2-3 times a night to pass urine, a weak stream that dribbles at the end, a sudden urge to go, and a feeling your bladder is not fully empty. You do NOT have fever, burning when passing urine, weight loss, poor appetite, lumps, bone or back pain, sore throat, recent heavy exercise, trauma, or lots of beetroot. You smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 30 years and quit 5 years ago. You worked with industrial dyes and rubber solvents years ago. You take aspirin and perindopril for blood pressure. No warfarin. Your idea: 'Is it my prostate, or is it cancer?' Your concern: cancer and needing an operation. Your expectation: a clear answer and a plan. Affect: anxious, cooperative, asks 'Doctor, is this serious?' Reveal risk factors (smoking, dye exposure) only if specifically asked.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP at a community practice. Barry Whitfield, 55, presents with visible red/pink urine. Take a focused, prioritised history over 6 minutes, then explain to the patient your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses, and outline your initial investigation plan. You do not need to perform a physical examination, but you may ask the examiner for specific examination findings. Pay attention to features that would make you worried about a serious underlying cause.
examiner_instructions: Award marks for a systematic haematuria history that actively screens for malignancy. The critical safety point: visible (macroscopic) haematuria in a man over 40 is urothelial/bladder cancer until proven otherwise and mandates urgent urology referral for cystoscopy PLUS upper-tract imaging (CT urography) regardless of a benign-feeling prostate. Candidates who label this 'just BPH' and stop should not pass the safety domain. Strong candidates elicit smoking and occupational dye/rubber exposure, quantify LUTS (voiding vs storage, consider IPSS), and note the patient is on aspirin. If the candidate asks for examination findings, provide: smooth, non-nodular enlarged prostate on DRE, dipstick positive for RBC, suprapubic dullness. Prompt once if they omit malignancy screening: 'Anything else in the history you would want to cover?'

criteria: Characterises haematuria (timing in stream, clots, painless vs painful, duration)
Screens malignancy risk: smoking, occupational dye/rubber/hydrocarbon exposure, prior pelvic radiotherapy/cyclophosphamide, schistosomiasis travel
Elicits and groups LUTS into voiding/obstructive vs storage/irritative (considers IPSS)
Covers infection, stones, GN (sore throat/flu), trauma, beetroot, bleeding tendency and anticoagulant/antiplatelet use
States BPH is a diagnosis of exclusion for haematuria and a benign DRE does not exclude cancer
Prioritises bladder/urothelial and renal cancer as must-exclude given age >40 and visible haematuria
Gives a structured differential (cancer, infection, stones, GN, prostate, pseudohaematuria)
Urgent urology referral for flexible cystoscopy PLUS upper-tract CT urography
Requests urine microscopy/culture and urine cytology, UEC, PSA, FBC/coagulation given aspirin
Does not falsely reassure the patient that a smooth prostate explains the blood
Addresses patient's cancer fear honestly without false reassurance
Explains diagnosis and plan in plain language, checks understanding, safety-nets

red_flags: Visible (macroscopic) haematuria in a man over 40 - bladder/urothelial cancer until proven otherwise, mandates urgent cystoscopy and CT urography
Clots and painless haematuria increase suspicion of an underlying tumour
Significant smoking history plus occupational aniline dye/rubber/hydrocarbon exposure (major bladder-cancer risk factors)
Constitutional symptoms (weight loss, bone/back pain) or a hard nodular prostate on DRE suggesting malignancy
Haematuria with fever, flank pain and rigors suggesting pyelonephritis/urosepsis requiring urgent treatment
australian_guidelines: eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines) - visible haematuria warrants investigation for urinary tract malignancy; do not attribute to BPH without exclusion
RACGP Red Book / RACGP guidance - macroscopic haematuria in adults over 40 requires urgent urological referral for cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging (CT urography)
PBS - alpha-blockers (e.g. tamsulosin) and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (e.g. finasteride) are PBS-listed for symptomatic BPH once malignancy is excluded
IPSS (International Prostate Symptom Score) recommended to quantify LUTS severity and guide BPH management
learning_objectives: Recognise that visible haematuria in a man over 40 mandates malignancy work-up regardless of prostate findings
Take a structured haematuria history covering the full differential (infection, stones, cancer, GN, prostate, pseudohaematuria)
Distinguish voiding/obstructive from storage/irritative LUTS and quantify with IPSS
Outline the Australian haematuria investigation pathway: urine MC&S and cytology, CT urography, flexible cystoscopy, UEC, PSA, coagulation
key_points: BPH is a diagnosis of exclusion for haematuria; a smooth, non-nodular prostate does not exclude bladder cancer.
Exercise can cause genuine transient haematuria (true RBCs); rhabdomyolysis causes myoglobinuria - a dipstick positive for blood with NO RBCs on microscopy - which is not haematuria.
Dysuria is uncommon in pure BPH; its presence should prompt a search for concurrent infection or bladder pathology.
Aspirin is an antiplatelet and rarely explains frank haematuria on its own - never let anticoagulation be the reason to skip investigation.
